summary:
Martinique stands under France's national framework. Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department in full, so identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime operate here as in the metropole. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1815, the 2013 marriage-equality law applies, and gender-marker change is available through the simplified judicial route introduced by the 2016-17 reforms.

Discrimination protection rests on several instruments that reach the island directly. Goods and services have been covered since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2), employment since Labour Code article L1132-1 in 2008, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, where the wording 'sexual identity' was replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. No Martinique-specific enforcement or litigation record for these provisions is documented in the sources available for this entry.

Hostile public speech is a criminal offence. A National Assembly amendment approved on 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic public comment illegal, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and up to 12 months' imprisonment, and amended the 1881 press-freedom law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence, and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. The first conviction under the provision, of MP Christian Vanneste in January 2006, was cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Penalties for physical assault or murder rise where the offence is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, and since 2017 transphobia has operated as an aggravating cause for all crimes punishable by prison.

Legal gender recognition operates on the island under the regime effective since 1 January 2017: no surgery and no medical diagnosis are required, but an application must still be made to a court to change the gender marker, while a first-name change can be handled at the registry office. The bill was signed on 18 November 2016 after passing the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly; the Constitutional Council ruled it constitutional on 17 November 2016 while dropping the original self-certification provision. Before that reform, legal gender change had been banned for decades until the 1992 European Court of Human Rights case B. v. France.

Prison is the sharpest documented risk for trans visitors. Under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, placement follows the gender marker on the detainee's identity documents rather than anatomy, which puts most trans women into all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them ('we don't want any women here'). The department's establishments operate under this same framework. France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, found on 25 May 2021 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on-site inspections in which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse; its recommendations cover placement, isolation, safety and staff training.

Healthcare is covered but uneven. Gender-affirming treatment is reimbursed by the Sécurité Sociale under the long-term-illness scheme ALD 31, and a 2022 ILGA-Europe report nonetheless documented significant problems, including extended waiting times and access that varies with location. Trans youth care is contested nationally: a report commissioned in March 2024 by centre-right Republican senators fed legislation to ban medical transition under 18, which passed the Senate in May 2024, was opposed by the Macron government and has had no recorded movement since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. The Académie Nationale de Médecine has characterised the rise in people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access.

Conversion therapy was banned by a bill published on 1 February 2022. Recorded anti-LGB(T) violence rose nationally by 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018, according to a report released on 16 May 2020. Community infrastructure exists on the island: JM Concept 972 runs information, meetings and services for Martinique's LGBT community, with events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September 2025, and the Rights in Exile (AsyLex) resource page lists local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts for the department.
tangentialFactors:
Several adjacent national measures reach Martinique without being trans-specific. Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state cover for women under 43, and the MSM blood-donation deferral was removed on 16 March 2022. Neither alters the identity-document or detention position a trans visitor would face, but both mark the direction of the national regime.

Legal history behind the current equality regime is worth carrying for context. The 1960 Mirguet amendment classified homosexuality as a 'national scourge' alongside alcoholism, and the Vichy law of 6 August 1942 set the age of consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones; the gap was narrowed to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. The 1992 B. v. France judgment ended the outright ban on legal gender change. Comparatively, France's route is judicial rather than purely administrative: several neighbouring systems of the same region have moved to registry-level self-declaration, and the French Constitutional Council's removal of self-declaration in 2016 is the specific constraint that keeps a court hearing in the process.

The contested national debate on youth gender care has no documented local counterpart. A 2022 ILGA-Europe assessment and the Académie Nationale de Médecine's cautionary position sit in tension over how access should be managed, and the practical effect in Martinique is likely to be felt mainly through waiting lists rather than through any island-specific restriction.
localsOnly:
Local community infrastructure on the island includes JM Concept 972, a Martinique lesbian, gay, bi and trans network that provides information, meetings and services, and runs private parties and garden parties with dated 2025 events; the Rights in Exile (AsyLex) page additionally lists AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM among organisations serving the overseas departments.

Residents are covered by national anti-bullying and education policy: the Ministry of Education launched the Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign in January 2019, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day, and in March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms.
outOfScopeNotes:
Several points remain unresolved in the sources assembled for this entry. There is no Martinique-specific data on how the gender-marker court route is applied on the island, including filing costs, hearing schedules or refusal rates; the 2016-17 reform is documented at national level only.

The CGLPL findings on transgender detainees rest on referrals and inspections conducted at mainland establishments (Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse). Whether its recommendations have been implemented at the department's own prisons is not sourced here, and the departmental prison population figures for trans detainees are not documented.

Enforcement figures for the 2004 hate-speech offence and for homophobic and transphobic aggravated penalties are national; no island breakdown appears in the record. The 36% rise in recorded attacks and insults is a national 2019 statistic and cannot be attributed to Martinique.

The status of the under-18 medical-transition bill after 23 July 2024 is unresolved in the sources, as is any local waiting-time or access data for gender-affirming care in Martinique beyond the national ALD 31 coverage position.
